newsitem.title: FRANCE: Belgium criticises France on eve of Chirac visit.
newsitem.headline: Belgium criticises France on eve of Chirac visit.

text.p: Belgium expressed irritation with France's industrial policies and border controls on the eve of a two-day visit from Wednesday by French President Jacques Chirac.
"We have to iron out differences," Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told the French daily Le Figaro in an interview released on Tuesday, a day ahead of publication.

Dehaene, whose nation is often at odds with its big southern neighbour, pointed to long-running disputes with France over the closure of a Renault car plant, French border checks and French refusal so far to hand over secret documents in a bribery case.
Chirac is hoping to smooth differences in talks with Dehaene and other Belgian leaders during the visit, the highest level contact between the two nations since 1991.
He will also reaffirm commitment to a single European currency in talks with European Commission President Jacques Santer on Thursday.

"This visit will be the chance to put these sensitive (bilateral) dossiers into perspective...to underline the closeness of our bilateral relations and joint commitment to deepening European construction," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.

He accused France's new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, swept to power in an upset June 1 election, of raising false hopes of halting the planned closure of a Renault SA car plant in Belgium employing 3,100 people.

"He said certain things during the election campaign about which I can only conclude that he was not speaking with the perspective of victory," Dehaene said. The French state is the biggest shareholder in Renault with 46 percent.

Dehaene, due to meet Chirac after his arrival on Wednesday afternoon, also said it would be "totally incomprehensible" if a bribery probe against French warplane maker Serge Dassault foundered over Paris' refusal to hand over secret documents.
"I don't understand very well the national strategic interest referred to," he said, adding that the Belgian statute of limitations threatened to curtail investigation in 1998.

Belgian police are investigating allegations that Dassault Aviation paid 600 million Belgian francs ($17 million) to political parties to secure a contract to fit air defence systems to Belgian F-16 jets in the late 1980s.

France's former centre-right government refused to hand over the documents but Jospin's government has said it is reviewing the request. An official at the French Justice Ministry said that a decision seemed unlikely during Chirac's visit.

Dehaene also said he felt a "certain shock" that France chose to invoke emergency rules to maintain land border controls against Belgium and Luxembourg despite the EU's so-called Schengen pact aimed at creating a border-free zone.

France says drug smugglers pass through the two countries from the Netherlands, which Paris accuses of having lax policies. Yet France has lifted border controls with Germany, its main EU ally, meaning traffickers can take a longer route from the Netherlands to France via Germany and avoid checks.

And Dehaene said the border, crossed by dozens of roads, was highly porous. "I invite you to accompany me across the French border. Lets take drugs with us if you like, and you will see how easily it is to get across," Dehaene said.
